purpose: Evaluate backend API E2E test authoring against a runnable repository fixture and real HTTP mutation oracle through Codex MCP.
workspaceState: Evidence was produced from the uncommitted live-benchmark diff that contains this file.
runner: codex mcp-server 0.145.0 over stdio + generated Go test + real HTTP mutation oracle
fidelity: ephemeral real Go HTTP process with file-backed owned state and sandbox-mail capture state

initialSixCallAB.transport: codex MCP; one fresh thread per call

initialOracle.finding: The three-mutant oracle had a false ceiling because it did not test delayed forbidden side effects.

optimization.change: Require a bounded stability window when asserting absence of asynchronous side effects; reject a single immediate snapshot as proof of absence.

conclusion.quality: The calibrated candidate improved from 88/96 to 96/96 and from 1/3 to 3/3 delayed-side-effect detection. It matches the locked baseline's artifact quality on this fixture.
conclusion.completion: The optimized candidate completed 3/3 MCP calls normally; the locked baseline completed 2/3 normally although all three artifacts passed.
conclusion.latency: Optimized candidate total latency was 528391ms versus 641948ms for baseline, but baseline includes one 240000ms timeout and the sample is too small for a stable speed claim.
conclusion.decision: Keep the asynchronous-absence contract change and the live mutation benchmark. Do not claim a general backend E2E quality advantage from one fixture.

limitations: This is one intentionally small Go backend fixture with three runs per compared variant, not a statistical production benchmark.

Codex model sandboxes could build the fixture but could not bind the loopback port; authoritative dynamic scoring was therefore executed by the outer real HTTP mutation oracle after each generated artifact was locked.
Codex MCP does not expose token usage in this tool response, so token counters are unavailable.
Raw MCP reports were not committed because progress notifications made them 7-15 MB; their hashes are retained and the runner now stores notification counts instead of payloads.
